Raca
RAY-kah
noun
From the Aramaic reyqa', “empty one, worthless fellow,” from a root signifying “to be empty, void, vain”; carried untranslated through the Greek of Matthew into the KJV, whose margin renders it “Vain fellow.”

Biblical Definition

Raca is a word of contempt — the Aramaic sneer that calls a man empty, a worthless nothing, a head with nothing in it. Our Lord takes it up in the Sermon on the Mount, where He drives the sixth commandment past the hand and into the heart. The scribes had heard it said by them of old time, “Thou shalt not kill” (Mat 5:21), and had made the law a fence about the outward act only: keep your knife sheathed and you are guiltless. Christ answers that the commandment reaches further than any court of men can follow. “Whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire” (Mat 5:22). Here is a rising scale — the anger nursed, the contempt spoken, the scorn that damns the soul — and every rung of it is murder in the sight of God. To call a brother Raca is to unmake him, to strike the image of God in him with the tongue, to pass a sentence of worthlessness upon one whom the LORD may have chosen from before the foundation of the world. Our Lord traces the whole traffic to its spring: “out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders” (Mat 15:19). The murderer’s work begins long before the blow, in the contempt that first empties a brother of his worth.

Webster 1828 Definition

A term of contempt: empty one, worthless fellow; the Aramaic sneer our Lord names as murder of the heart.

expand to see more

RACA, a Syriac or Aramaic word of contempt, signifying empty, vain, worthless.

The KJV margin renders it “Vain fellow” (Mat 5:22).

It is a sneer that pronounces a brother of no account.

Our Lord ranks it with murder under the sixth commandment.

It is spoken by the tongue but conceived in the heart (Mat 15:19).

Key Scripture

Mat 5:21 — "Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not kill; and whosoever shall kill shall be in danger of the judgment:"

Mat 5:22 — "But I say unto you, That whosoever is angry with his brother without a cause shall be in danger of the judgment: and whosoever shall say to his brother, Raca, shall be in danger of the council: but whosoever shall say, Thou fool, shall be in danger of hell fire."

Mat 15:19 — "For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies:"

Jas 3:9 — "Therewith bless we God, even the Father; and therewith curse we men, which are made after the similitude of God."

Modern Corruption

The age reduces the sixth commandment to bare outward murder; Christ Himself extends it to the angry heart and the contemptuous tongue.

expand to see more

The corruption here is ancient and thoroughly modern at once: the reduction of the sixth commandment to the bare outward act. The scribes taught that a man who had shed no blood had kept the law, and the age agrees with them — it reckons itself innocent of murder because it has never lifted a hand, while it slays with the tongue daily and calls the slaughter opinion. Christ forecloses that defence. He puts the anger, the Raca, and the “Thou fool” on one continuous ladder with the knife, and hangs hell fire at the end of it. The law of God is spiritual; it binds the heart, and no man who has despised his brother may plead a clean hand.

The sneer is a doctrine as well as a sin. To say Raca is to declare a man empty — a nothing, of no account, worthless — and that is a lie against Genesis 1:27, for the brother so dismissed bears the image of God, and may be a vessel of mercy afore prepared unto glory. James marks the contradiction: with the same tongue we bless God and curse men, which are made after the similitude of God (Jas 3:9). The remedy is not a stricter guard upon the lips but a new heart, out of which the evil thought no longer proceeds. Christ, who was Himself despised and rejected, took the contempt of men upon the tree; the sinner who has said Raca to his brother must go to Him for pardon, and having been pardoned, learn to see his brother as God sees him.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means an empty one, a worthless fellow — a spoken sneer of contempt.

expand to see more

Raca — from the Aramaic reyqa', “empty, vain, worthless.”

It is left untranslated in the Greek text and in the KJV.

The KJV margin explains it: “Vain fellow.”

It names a brother as a nothing, a head with nothing in it.

Christ ranks it with murder under the sixth commandment (Mat 5:22).

Usage

"To say Raca is to call a brother empty — and to strike the image of God with the tongue."

"The sixth commandment reaches past the hand to the angry heart and the contemptuous word."

"Anger, Raca, and “Thou fool” are rungs of one ladder, and hell fire hangs at the end."
